title: Evaluating Doctrines
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up the Kalama Sutta, in which the Buddha, camped outside Kesaputta, tells villagers confused by rival teachers not to rely on tradition, scripture, logic, or a speaker's charisma. Norman reads the sutra through, including the four assurances of a mind free of ill will, and notes that people citing it for self-verification often skip its call to check with community and the wise. The reason is plain: we may be unreliable judges, enjoying a teaching because it matches our preconceptions. Norman closes on loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, which family members would confirm by saying "you're such a much nicer person now."

sentences.text: This morning I want to start with a sutra from the Pali collection.
It's something the Buddha taught when he was traveling around and he came to the country of the Kalamas.
He was organizing himself, as he often did, outside town, making camp, outside the town of Kesaputta.
By this time he was pretty well known, so when the Buddha was coming to town people were aware of it and they wanted to come and receive teachings and ask questions.
Some people from Kesaputta came to visit him and they bowed and they made the usual greetings and obeisance.
Then they said to him these words:
*There are, Lord, some ascetics and Brahmins who come to Kesaputta and they explain and elucidate their own doctrines, but disparage, debunk, revile and vilify the doctrines of others.
But then some other ascetics and Brahmins come to Kesaputta and they too explain and elucidate their own doctrines, but disparage, debunk, revile and vilify the doctrines of others.
So this puts us into doubt.
We're confused.
We have perplexity as to which of these good ascetics speaks the truth and which speak falsehood.*
So the Buddha said to them:
*Well, it makes sense that you would be confused.
It is fitting that you would be perplexed.
Oh Kalamas, it is fitting for you to be in doubt.
Do not go by oral traditions.

Do not go by lineage of teaching, by hearsay, by a collection of scriptures, by logical reasoning, by inferential reasoning, by reflection on reasons, by the acceptance of a view after pondering it, by the seeming competence of the speaker, or because you think this ascetic is our teacher.
Those are not the bases on which you should judge the truth or falseness of a teaching.
But only when you know for yourselves: these things are blamable.
These things are censured by the wise.
These things, if undertaken and practiced, lead to harm and suffering.*
*If that's the case, you should abandon these teachings.
If, on the other hand, you come to see by your own experience: these things are wholesome.
These things are blameless.
These things are practiced by the wise.
These things, if undertaken and practiced, lead to welfare and happiness, then you should engage those teachings.*
And he went on:
*Kalamas, a person who is greedy, hating and deluded, overpowered by greed, hatred and delusion, has thoughts controlled by greed, hatred and delusion.
And that person will eventually take life, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, tell lies,*
and other, I think, bad things are implied.
*And that person will encourage others to do likewise.
So in a case like that, is this going to lead to harm and suffering for a long time or not, Kalamas?*
And they think about it and they say, yeah, that's going to lead to a lot of trouble.
Then the Buddha considered the opposite case:

*That noble disciple who doesn't have greed, doesn't have ill will, is not confused, clearly comprehending, always mindful, if there's a person like that, who then dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving kindness, pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with compassion, pervading one corner with a mind imbued with altruistic joy, pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with equanimity, imbued with equanimity.
And after infusing the first quarter with these things, then infusing the second quarter and the third quarter and the fourth quarter, all around infusing the whole world with these four attitudes.
What about that?*
And they say, that would be good.
That would lead to good.
That would be much better.
Then the Buddha goes on further:
*When, Kalamas, this noble disciple has thus made his mind free of enmity, free of ill will, uncorrupted and pure, he has won four assurances in this very life.
The first assurance is this.

If there is another world, and if good and bad deeds bear fruit and yield result in that other world, it is possible that with the breakup of the body after death, I shall arise in a good destination and in a heavenly world.*
*That's the first assurance.
The second assurance is this.

If there is no other world, and if good and bad deeds do not bear fruit and yield results in the future, still, right here, in this very world, in this very life, I will live happily and free of enmity and ill will.
The third assurance is this.
Suppose evil befalls the evildoer.*
Suppose, in other words, you do bad things and there's a future bad result.
*Then, as I do not intend evil for anyone, how can suffering afflict me, one who does no evil deed?
The fourth assurance is this.
Suppose evil does not befall the evildoer.
Then, right here, I see myself purified anyway.*

So this is a pretty famous sutra that I'm sure many of you have heard before, and it's the sutra that is usually cited when someone wants to make the point that the Buddha was a very practical teacher and was free from preconceived doctrines and ideas and that he only taught what works.

He's saying here, pretty straightforwardly, that no matter how impressive or logical or beautiful a teaching is, no matter how charismatic or enlightened or intelligent the speaker is, no matter how fabulous and ancient and well-respected the tradition that the teaching comes from is, no matter how much faith you have in the tradition and the teacher, even if it's your own teacher, you should not accept the teaching until you confirm for yourself that it will lead to good results in your life.
Good results here seem specifically to mean that when you put these practices into action, you will see a reduction in harm and unhappiness in your life and an increase in happiness and well-being.
You have to find this out for yourself in your own life.
You're the only one who can verify this for yourself.

So this is the point of the teachings, he's implying: not that they're true or wonderful or interesting or inspiring or correct or not correct, but that when put into practice they will lead to reduction of suffering and increase of happiness.

The other thing we should learn from this, if you are yourself a spiritual teacher going around espousing views and doctrines: don't debunk and vilify the views of others, because that will confuse people and you don't want to confuse people.
But anyway, this is mostly from the point of view of those who are receiving teachings.
This is how you tell when you hear a bunch of conflicting views and you're trying to figure out which is true or not true.
You don't need to worry about figuring it out.
Just put them all into practice and see which ones will lead to a benefit for you and which ones won't.
And that's the proof.

When people want to say how great Buddhism is in this regard and it doesn't require faith and all this or belief in anything, they usually cite this sutra and they usually don't notice the part that says that besides confirming this for yourself, the teachings should also be acceptable to the community and they should also be confirmed as positive teachings by the wise.
It also says that they should not be blameworthy and they should be approved, not reproved, by the wise.
And that we, ourselves, should make the effort to see that this is so.
Usually, as I say, they don't mention this passage.
And with some justice, the main point clearly is verify for yourself in your life, but he also mentions these other things.
That tells us that it's a little more subtle than usually we think.
We kind of fold it into our ideology of rugged individualism by not for yourself and all this.
And yes, but more than that, there's a social dimension to the teaching.
Because the problem is, see, this is the problem with relying on yourself.
What if you're unreliable?
What if you, yourself, are actually unreliable?
And let's be honest, we're somewhat reliable and somewhat unreliable, all of us, and we might be quite a bit weighted on the unreliable side.
By which I mean, simply, that we might have strong preferences and therefore strong blindnesses.
Maybe we are fully capable of really thinking that we're confirming a teaching for ourselves, when in fact we're just enjoying this teaching because we agreed with it to begin with.
It perfectly fit our preconceptions.
So therefore it's easy for us to imagine that it's working beautifully, even though it's not.
We're not actually being honest with ourselves.
To assure that we are seeing clearly, the Buddha says, you should also check this out with your friends and the community and also check your common sense.
Does this sound like a reasonable, decent teaching?
Do the people that you know in your community support it and confirm it?
Do the wise people in the community, particularly, see it as a good teaching?
Now, I think it's possible that we could be wrong about all of it.
We could be so blind that we could say, oh yes, everybody thinks it's a good teaching, and all the wise people think it's good too, but they're all looking at you like, but you don't notice that.
So it's possible we could still be wrong, but it does sort of help if we are told, well, check it out a little further.
This is very sensible, it seems to me.
As we read, the Buddha then goes on to have a dialogue with the Kalamas about exactly what these good or bad effects on our life would look like.
He says, when you yourself or someone that you see is full of greedy thoughts, full of ill will, and has lots of confused ideas, we do act based on the way we think, right?
That's why the way we think is so important.

So that person is going to be doing greedy, nasty, confused actions, breaking precepts right and left, all the canons of decent conduct, harming other people, lying, deranging his mind with all kinds of substances, and acting out of that.
He's using sexuality, creating disturbances, havoc in the community, because his mind is so full of greedy, deluded, hateful thoughts, which are bound eventually to lead to these bad actions.
So the Buddha says, well, that's what I'm talking about.
When a teaching doesn't challenge those thoughts and only encourages them or leaves them alone and that kind of stuff happens, is that a good thing?
Does that lead to happiness?
No, it doesn't.
It leads to more harm, more unhappiness.
Then the Buddha paints a portrait on the other side.
What about the person who practices mindfulness, who pays attention to her thoughts?
She realizes that when greedy thoughts are present, hateful and deluded thoughts, those thoughts have bad consequences, lead to bad behaviors and unhappiness.
And so when those thoughts arise in the mind, because one can't decide, as we read the other day, you can't say let the mind be like this and it'll be like that.
No, the mind is going to be the way it is.
We can't make it be a certain way, but when the mind arises and we understand this is a mind of greed, ill will, delusion, then we have to forbear.
We have to just not be acting on that mind, not let that mind grab hold of us.
Just forbear because we know where that's taking us and we don't want to go there.

So instead of encouraging such thoughts, that person is actively forbearing those thoughts, not getting hooked by them, and actively encouraging loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy and equanimity.
And she imagines that she is suffusing those positive thoughts, as we chant, over the entire universe.
So the Buddha depicts such a person and says, okay, well, what about a person like that, how will that be?
Yeah, there's going to be way less harm and way more benefit and way more happiness for that person and her friends and her community and the whole world than in the opposite case.
So the Buddha is saying, I'm not here to give you beautiful doctrines and ideas, I'm just telling you, check this out for yourself, see if that's true.
Test it out and see, and you'll notice also that when you practice these things, most of the people in your community will say, yeah, that seems like a good idea, love you, I think that's good.
Not being greedy, not being hateful, yeah, I support that.
I think the wise people also will support all that.
They will not disapprove of you if you are committed to benefit for others, kindness, compassion.
So just to say a word about these four, I'm sure we all know them very well and have practiced them a lot over the years.

But just to note that it's really such a hopeful and radical thought of the Buddha that we are capable of intentionally and even somewhat systematically cultivating beneficial thoughts and attitudes and little by little through cultivation replacing the usual crappy thoughts and attitudes with more beneficial ones.
That we actually have the capacity to do that.
We don't need to be stuck for our whole life with thoughts and attitudes that we think come naturally and that's just who I am and how I look at things.
We don't need to be stuck with that really.
And if we think that we're stuck with it, we're actually deciding to continue with it because we don't have to.
If you practice, intentionally practice compassion, you can increase your capacity to be compassionate and caring for your own troubles and the troubles of others.
If you directly confront your jealousy or indifference at the good fortune of others and instead intentionally cultivate joy when others are joyful, you can increase your own joy and happiness.

And if you can little by little even out your mind even if it goes wild with attachment or aversion, so that you can have compassion, loving kindness and sympathetic joy more equally for everyone, not just the people you're concerned with but more equally for everyone including yourself, then little by little you can become a steady, solid, caring human being.
You could actually over time develop this if you want.

So I hope and assume that everybody here has long ago taken the Buddha's advice on this point and has been cultivating these practices over time, and you would have seen for yourself exactly what he's saying, that it will have positive effects on your life.
And certainly, again, the wise would approve of this, and everybody in your family would say, yeah, you're such a much nicer person now.
You were so difficult to live with before.
What a good idea to be a kinder person.
I'm in favor of it.
In fact, when we inquire, I think we do discover we don't really need to take a big international survey.
I think we already know that these qualities of kindness, compassion, caring, non-greed, non-hatred, that these qualities are universally praised by humanity.
